claims.label: Theorem 1
claims.statement_original:
Under Condition 1, as $\min(n,p_1,\ldots,p_K)\to\infty$, the limits of
\[
p^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B)(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B+\lambda\boldsymbol I_p)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad p^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B)(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B+\lambda\boldsymbol I_p)^{-2}\boldsymbol\Sigma\}\tag{2}
\]
are zeros and the limit of
\[
p^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B)(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B+\lambda\boldsymbol I_p)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B)(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_B+\lambda\boldsymbol I_p)^{-1}\}\tag{3}
\]
is $\omega^{-1}\sum_{l,h=1,\ldots,K;\ l\ne h}\omega_l\omega_h\cdot\{1-\lambda m_l(-\lambda)\}\{1-\lambda m_h(-\lambda)\}+o_p(1)$, where
\[
m_l(z)=\int\frac1{t\{1-\omega_l-\omega_lzm_l(z)\}-z}\,dH_l(t),\tag{4}
\]
in which $H_l(t)$ is the LSD of $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{B_l}$ and $m_l(z)$ is the Stieltjes transform of $M_l(x)$ for $l=1,\ldots,K$.

claims.label: Theorem 2
claims.statement_original:
Under polygenic model (1) and Conditions 1 - 4, as $\min(n,n_z,p_l)\to\infty$, the limit of $A_B^2(\lambda)$ is
\[
\frac{[1-\lambda\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda)]^2\cdot h_\beta^4}{[1+\lambda^2\boldsymbol R_2(\lambda)-2\lambda\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda)+\boldsymbol R_3(\lambda)]\cdot h_\beta^2+[\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda)-\lambda\boldsymbol R_2(\lambda)]\cdot\omega(1-h_\beta^2)}+o_p(1),
\]
where
\[
\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_l\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\},
\]
\[
\boldsymbol R_2(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_l\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-2}(\boldsymbol I_{p_l}-\dot a_l\boldsymbol\Sigma_l)\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\},\qquad\text{and}
\]
\[
\boldsymbol R_3(\lambda)=\omega^{-1}\sum_{l,h=1,\ldots,K;\ l\ne h}\omega_l\omega_h\{1-\lambda m_l(-\lambda)\}\{1-\lambda m_h(-\lambda)\}.
\]
Here $a_l$ is the unique positive solution of
\[
1-a_l=\omega_l\cdot\left\{1-\lambda\int_0^\infty(a_lt+\lambda)^{-1}\,dH_l(t)\right\}=\omega_l\cdot\left\{1-\mathrm E_{H_l(t)}\left(\frac\lambda{a_lt+\lambda}\right)\right\}
\]
and $\dot a_l$ is the first order derivative of $a_l$ and given by
\[
\dot a_l=\frac{\omega_l\cdot\mathrm E_{H_l(t)}\left\{\frac{a_lt}{(a_lt+\lambda)^2}\right\}}{-1-\omega_l\lambda\cdot\mathrm E_{H_l(t)}\left\{\frac t{(a_lt+\lambda)^2}\right\}}.
\]
When $\lambda=\lambda^*\equiv\omega\cdot(1-h_\beta^2)/h_\beta^2$, $A_B^2(\lambda)$ is maximized and the optimal prediction accuracy is given by
\[
A_B^2(\lambda^*)=h_\beta^2\cdot\frac{\{1-\lambda^*\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda^*)\}^2}{1-\lambda^*\boldsymbol R_1(\lambda^*)+\boldsymbol R_3(\lambda^*)}+o_p(1).\tag{5}
\]

claims.label: Theorem 3
claims.statement_original:
Under Condition 1, as $\min(n_w,p_l)\to\infty$, the limit of $p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{BW_l}+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{BW_l}+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}$ is approximated by
\[
p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\left[1-\frac{n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}}{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2}\right]^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\},
\]
where $\boldsymbol K_l=[1+n^{-1}\mathrm E\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{BW_l}+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l=\lambda v_{w_l}(-\lambda)\boldsymbol\Sigma_l$. In addition, the limit of $p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{BW_l}+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{BW_l}+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\}$ is approximated by
\[
p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\frac{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2\cdot \operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\}}{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2-n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}}.
\]

claims.label: Theorem 4
claims.statement_original:
Under polygenic model (1) and Conditions 1, 2, 3, and 5, as $\min(n,n_w,n_z,p_l)\to\infty$, we have
\[
A_{BW}^2(\lambda)=\frac{\boldsymbol Q_1^2(\lambda)\cdot h_\beta^4}{\boldsymbol Q_2(\lambda)\cdot h_\beta^2+\boldsymbol Q_3(\lambda)\cdot\omega}+o_p(1),
\]
where $\boldsymbol Q_1(\lambda)$, $\boldsymbol Q_2(\lambda)$, and $\boldsymbol Q_3(\lambda)$ are, respectively, given by
\[
p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_{w_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\},
\]
\[
p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\frac{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2\cdot \operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\}}{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2-n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}},
\]
and
\[
p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\left[1-\frac{n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}}{[1+n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}]^2}\right]^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\{(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l(\boldsymbol K_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}.
\]
Here $a_{w_l}$ is the unique positive solution of $1-a_{w_l}=\omega_{w_l}\cdot\{1-\lambda\int_0^\infty(a_{w_l}t+\lambda)^{-1}\,dH_l(t)\}$. In addition, we have
\[
A_{BZ}^2(\lambda)=\frac{\{1-\lambda\boldsymbol Q_4(\lambda)\}^2\cdot h_\beta^4}{\{\boldsymbol Q_5(\lambda)-\lambda\boldsymbol Q_6(\lambda)\}\cdot h_\beta^2+\{\boldsymbol Q_4(\lambda)-\lambda\boldsymbol Q_7(\lambda)\}\cdot\omega}+o_p(1),
\]
where
\[
\boldsymbol Q_4(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\},\qquad\boldsymbol Q_5(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\},
\]
\[
\boldsymbol Q_6(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-2}(\boldsymbol I_{p_l}-\dot a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l)\boldsymbol\Sigma_l^2\},\qquad\text{and}
\]
\[
\boldsymbol Q_7(\lambda)=p^{-1}\sum_{l=1}^K\operatorname{tr}\{(a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l+\lambda\boldsymbol I_{p_l})^{-2}(\boldsymbol I_{p_l}-\dot a_{z_l}\boldsymbol\Sigma_l)\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}.
\]
Moreover, $a_{z_l}$ is the unique positive solution of $1-a_{z_l}=\omega_{z_l}\cdot\{1-\lambda\int_0^\infty(a_{z_l}t+\lambda)^{-1}\,dH_l(t)\}$ and $\dot a_{z_l}$ is the first order derivative of $a_{z_l}$, given by
\[
\dot a_{z_l}=\frac{\omega_{z_l}\cdot\mathrm E_{H_l(t)}\left\{\frac{a_{z_l}t}{(a_{z_l}t+\lambda)^2}\right\}}{-1-\omega_{z_l}\cdot\lambda\mathrm E_{H_l(t)}\left\{\frac t{(a_{z_l}t+\lambda)^2}\right\}}.
\]

members.local_label: Section 2.1 — training, testing and reference data
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — training, testing and reference data
members.statement_original:
Consider two independent GWAS that are conducted for the same continuous complex trait with the same $p$ genetic variants:

Training GWAS: $(\boldsymbol X,\boldsymbol y)$, where $\boldsymbol X=(\boldsymbol x_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol x_p)\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb R^{n\times1}$;

Testing GWAS: $(\boldsymbol Z,\boldsymbol y_z)$, where $\boldsymbol Z=(\boldsymbol z_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol z_p)\in\mathbb R^{n_z\times p}$ and $\boldsymbol y_z\in\mathbb R^{n_z\times1}$.

Here $\boldsymbol y$ and $\boldsymbol y_z$ are the complex traits measured in two independent cohorts with sample sizes $n$ and $n_z$, respectively.

In addition, we define an external genotype reference panel dataset for the same $p$ genetic variants as

Genotype reference panel: $\boldsymbol W=(\boldsymbol w_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol w_p)\in\mathbb R^{n_w\times p}$.

interfaces.name: Uniformly bounded eigenvalues
interfaces.type_shape: Common deterministic covariance, standardized iid innovation entries with a fourth moment, and dimension-uniform spectral bounds. Preserve the source equation of population diagonal-one with column standardization without claiming their finite-sample equivalence.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Common deterministic covariance, standardized iid innovation entries with a fourth moment, and dimension-uniform spectral bounds. Preserve the source equation of population diagonal-one with column standardization without claiming their finite-sample equivalence.

members.statement_original: (a). Let $\boldsymbol X=\boldsymbol X_0\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}$, $\boldsymbol Z=\boldsymbol Z_0\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}$, and $\boldsymbol W=\boldsymbol W_0\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}$, where the entries of $\boldsymbol X_0$, $\boldsymbol Z_0$, and $\boldsymbol W_0$ are real-value i.i.d. random variables with mean zero, variance one, and a finite 4th order moment. The $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ is a $p\times p$ population level deterministic positive definite matrix of $p$ genetic variants. We have uniformly bounded eigenvalues in $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ in the sense that $0<c\leq\lambda_{\min}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)\leq\lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)\leq C$ for all $p$ and some constants $c,C$, where $\lambda_{\min}(\boldsymbol A)$ and $\lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol A)$ are the smallest and largest eigenvalues of a generic matrix $\boldsymbol A$, respectively. The $\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}$ denotes any nonnegative square root of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. For simplicity, we also assume $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{ii}=1$, $i=1,\ldots,p$, or equivalently, $\boldsymbol X$, $\boldsymbol Z$, and $\boldsymbol W$ have been column-standardized.

members.statement_original: (b). The $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ has a block-diagonal structure with $K$ blocks, whose boundaries are known, denoted by $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\operatorname{Diag}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol\Sigma_l,\ldots,\boldsymbol\Sigma_K)$, where $\boldsymbol\Sigma_l$ is a $p_l\times p_l$ matrix for $l\in1,\ldots,K$ such that $\sum_{l=1}^Kp_l=p$. Let $\boldsymbol X_l=(\boldsymbol x_{\widetilde p_{l-1}+1},\ldots,\boldsymbol x_{\widetilde p_l})$, $\boldsymbol W_l=(\boldsymbol w_{\widetilde p_{l-1}+1},\ldots,\boldsymbol w_{\widetilde p_l})$, and $\boldsymbol Z_l=(\boldsymbol z_{\widetilde p_{l-1}+1},\ldots,\boldsymbol z_{\widetilde p_l})$ be the submatrices of $\boldsymbol X$, $\boldsymbol W$, and $\boldsymbol Z$ corresponding to $\boldsymbol\Sigma_l$, respectively, where $\widetilde p_l=p_1+\cdots+p_l$.

interfaces.name: Empirical spectral distribution · Limiting spectral distribution
interfaces.type_shape: Population ESDs and assumed weak limits, distinct from the sample spectral laws M_l and M_w_l. Preserve the probability-distribution interpretation of H_l and H.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Population ESDs and assumed weak limits, distinct from the sample spectral laws M_l and M_w_l. Preserve the probability-distribution interpretation of H_l and H.

members.statement_original: (c). For $l=1,\ldots,K$, we define the empirical spectral distribution (ESD) of $\boldsymbol\Sigma_l$ as $F_{p_l}^{\boldsymbol\Sigma_l}(x)=p_l^{-1}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{p_l}\mathrm I(\lambda_i(\boldsymbol\Sigma_l)\leq x)$, $x\in\mathbb R$, where $\lambda_i(\boldsymbol A)$ is the $i$-th eigenvalue of a generic matrix $\boldsymbol A$. As $p_l\to\infty$, let $\{\boldsymbol\Sigma_l\}_{p_l>1}$ be a sequence of matrices, we assume that the sequence of corresponding ESDs $\{F_{p_l}^{\boldsymbol\Sigma_l}(x)\}_{p_l>1}$ converges weakly to a limit probability distribution $H_l(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R$, called the limiting spectral distribution (LSD), for each $l$. Similarly, we assume the $p\times p$ population level correlation matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ has a LSD, denoted as $H(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.

interfaces.name: Linear additive polygenic models
interfaces.type_shape: Two response equations with a shared effect vector, m causal coordinates and separate errors. Random-effect distribution and proportional causal count are later conditions, not imposed by these equations alone.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Two response equations with a shared effect vector, m causal coordinates and separate errors. Random-effect distribution and proportional causal count are later conditions, not imposed by these equations alone.

members.statement_original:
Without loss of generality, it is assumed that there are $m\leq p$ causal variants with nonzero effects and $\boldsymbol X_{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ and $\boldsymbol Z_{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{n_z\times m}$ denote the corresponding data matrices among the $p$ genetic variants in $\boldsymbol X$ and $\boldsymbol Z$, respectively. The linear additive polygenic models [Jiang et al., 2016] assume
\[
\boldsymbol y=\boldsymbol X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon=\boldsymbol X_{(1)}\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}+\boldsymbol\epsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boldsymbol y_z=\boldsymbol Z\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon_z=\boldsymbol Z_{(1)}\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}+\boldsymbol\epsilon_z,\tag{1}
\]
where $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}$ is a $m\times1$ vector of nonzero causal genetic effects, $\boldsymbol\beta$ is a $p\times1$ vector consisting of $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}$ and $p-m$ zeros, and $\boldsymbol\epsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_z$ represent independent random error vectors.

interfaces.type_shape: Centered finite-fourth-moment effect distribution with covariance scaled by p^{-1}, independent of the designs, and separate noise covariance matrices. The generic F notation is not a Gaussian assumption and does not itself enforce iid coordinates.

members.statement_original:
Let $F(0,V)$ represent a generic distribution with mean zero, (co)variance $V$, and finite fourth order moments. We assume that the distribution of $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}$ is independent of the genetic variant data $\boldsymbol X$, $\boldsymbol Z$, and $\boldsymbol W$ and satisfies $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}\sim F(\boldsymbol0,p^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol\Sigma_\beta)$, where $\boldsymbol\Sigma_\beta=\sigma_\beta^2\cdot\boldsymbol I_m$. In addition, $\boldsymbol\epsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_z$ are independent random variables satisfying
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\epsilon\\\boldsymbol\epsilon_z\end{pmatrix}\sim F\left[\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol0\\\boldsymbol0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\epsilon\epsilon}&\boldsymbol0\\\boldsymbol0&\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\epsilon_z\epsilon_z}\end{pmatrix}\right],
\]
where $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\epsilon\epsilon}=\sigma_\epsilon^2\cdot\boldsymbol I_n$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\epsilon_z\epsilon_z}=\sigma_{\epsilon_z}^2\cdot\boldsymbol I_{n_z}$.

naming_context.text: Next, we introduce the condition on nonzero genetic effects $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}$ and random error vectors $\boldsymbol\epsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_z$.

application_context.text: In Condition 3, we model $\boldsymbol\beta_{(1)}$ as i.i.d. random variables with finite moments [Dobriban and Wager, 2018, Jiang et al., 2016], reflecting the fact that most of genetic variants have a small contribution to complex traits in GWAS.

members.source_heading: Section 3 — training sample spectral law and transform
members.statement_original: The ESD of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{B_l}$ is denoted by $F_{p_l}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{B_l}}(x)=p_l^{-1}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{p_l}\mathrm I(\lambda_i(\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{B_l})\leq x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. As $p_l\to\infty$, it is well-known [Yao et al., 2015] that $F_{p_l}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{B_l}}(x)$ converges weakly to the LSD of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{B_l}$, denoted as $M_l(x)$, with probability one. The Stieltjes transform of $M_l(x)$, denoted as $m_l(z)$, can be implicitly defined by the Marchenko-Pastur equation given in equation (4) below [Bai and Zhou, 2008, Marchenko and Pastur, 1967, Silverstein, 1995].
